segments.caption: Same juice bottles, same score of -2. The z-test says reject. The t-test says don't.
So who's right? Here's z-test versus t-test, the complete comparison. Save this one!
Here are the textbook definitions.
A z-test compares a sample mean with a population mean, when the population standard deviation is known.
A t-test does the same, when it's unknown and has to be estimated from the sample.
The formulas differ by one letter.
z divides by sigma, the true population spread. t divides by s, the spread estimated from the sample.
An estimate adds extra uncertainty, especially when the sample is small.
That's why the t curve has fatter tails.
With 2 degrees of freedom, the tails are very fat. With 5, thinner. By 30, t is almost the normal curve.
Degrees of freedom, n - 1, tell you which t curve to use.
Now watch the 5% cut-off shrink as the sample grows.
And with infinite data: 1.96. The z value. t becomes z.
Back to our puzzle. A score of -2 only beats the t cut-off with more than 60 degrees of freedom.
9 bottles: fail to reject. 100 bottles: reject. Both tests were right, for what they knew.
The t-test wasn't wrong. It was more careful, because 9 bottles can't pin down the spread.
So which one should you use? Ask one question: do you know sigma?
Yes: z-test. No: t-test, at any sample size. And with a big sample, the two give almost the same answer.
Interview trap: use z when n is over 30. That's a rule of thumb, not the definition.
The real question is whether you know sigma. In practice, you rarely do, so t is the default.
And with a big sample, s gets very close to sigma. That's why z works as an approximation there.
So where is the z-test really used? Proportions.
In an A/B test, or a poll, the spread comes from the proportion itself, so we use z. 10% versus 12% conversion? That's a z-test.
Its standard error is the square root of p times 1 - p, over n. No sigma needed.
The same cut-offs build confidence intervals: ±1.96 with z, ±the t value with t.
That's why a small-sample t interval is always a little wider.
